tweets.text: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative. And for the sake of clarity and as I outlined on the pod, I think Anthropic has deep competitive advantages and is an amazing company. Ironically, the main risk I saw to Anthropic a few months ago was nationalization as a result of Dario’s own rhetoric and behavior. — https://nitter.kareem.one/GavinSBaker/status/2088611616577253502#m

v nice side efvent 0xturbanurban (@0xturbanurban) Yesterday evening I had the pleasure of attending an interesting event hosted by @sfcompute and @jumptrading focused on the compute space. Some brief takeaways: - There's an increasing understanding that greater liquidity in compute markets requires the construction of unifying benchmark indices, so that bespoke/OTC markets can be priced/quoted as a diff to a shared set of benchmarks, similar to what exists in the energy complex already (think crude grades and power). Part of the discussion is whether this will organically emerge if more traditional players (Citadel, Jump, blue-chip banks) expand their OTC offering for bilateral hedges (using their own prices), or require an independent party (S&P, CME, etc.) to validate and give credence for broader adoption. - Massive growth in the compute space is largely underpinned by structured financing trades with hedging mandates (similar to what you see in the oil and gas space). If someone with a sizable balance sheet just lent you a lot of money, who's likely to give you more aggressive pricing than their sales and trading arm? - Funding from life insurers has been a key part of the data center buildout (you could call it duration matching), with an increasing number of insurers considering hedging compute. Some of this exposure sits in mortgage books, while the biggest bucket is via corporate bonds ( $ORCL , $MSFT , $META , and $GOOG comprise nearly 80% of Athene's IG software debt). - Quite a few folks seem offered over on the backend of the curve, largely driven by: * Concerns that distressed sellers could flood the market if the AI growth story slows down (as there's a lot of GPU-backed debt to unwind) * Natural hedgers are mostly sellers, as operators need contracted revenue to borrow, so they sell further out on the curve; buyers mostly lock in near-term rates w/ marginal demand coming from a handful of labs whose spending is contingent on their ability to still tap into financing * Software improvements are reducing GPU-hour needs, all the while new chips are depreciating the value of old hardware per unit of compute: $NVDA is releasing a new gen roughly every year (Blackwell Ultra, Rubin, and Rubin Ultra). That said, it does look like old chips are staying useful longer than most depreciation models assume, since inference and smaller models still allow sufficient monetization of older hardware. It'll be quite exciting to see how the space continues to mature, especially as new marketplaces begin to emerge for financially and physically settled compute. Huge thanks to @affaan and team for organizing! — https://nitter.kareem.one/0xturbanurban/status/2110342060100264009#m

highlights.text_fr: Aujourd'hui, nous avons annoncé la découverte, menée par Claude, d'une machine moléculaire qui pourrait représenter un nouveau mécanisme d'édition génétique. Sa fonction précise, son utilité biotechnologique (le cas échéant) ou son niveau de signification ne sont pas encore clairs, mais c'est un travail dont j'aurais été fier en tant qu'étudiant en doctorat. Le travail a été principalement, mais pas entièrement, réalisé par Claude : notre équipe de sciences de la vie a suggéré un large domaine de recherche, Claude a parcouru la littérature et de nombreuses données génomiques pour découvrir quelque chose d'intéressant, puis Claude a proposé des expériences pour vérifier la découverte et notre équipe les a menées à bien. Il est facile de rejeter cela comme un événement isolé ou une simple curiosité, mais nous avons observé à plusieurs reprises une tendance où la performance de l'IA dans de nouveaux domaines intellectuels passe de faible à surhumaine en quelques années. En 2023, les modèles avaient du mal à faire des maths au niveau d'un lycéen moyen. En 2024, ils ont commencé à bien réussir les concours de maths pour les meilleurs lycéens du pays, en 2025 ils ont commencé à résoudre des problèmes ouverts mineurs, début 2026 des problèmes ouverts plus significatifs, et fin 2026 ils commencent à résoudre quelques-uns des problèmes ouverts les plus importants en mathématiques. Nous pensons que l'IA pour la biologie suit une tendance exponentielle similaire. La principale différence entre la biologie et les mathématiques, bien sûr, est que les maths peuvent être faites purement théoriquement, tandis que la biologie nécessite de l'expérimentation. Certains ont utilisé cela pour en déduire que l'utilité de l'IA en biologie sera limitée. Nous pensons que c'est faux. Comme nous l'avons démontré aujourd'hui, les humains peuvent collaborer avec l'IA pour réaliser les expériences, valider les résultats clés en quelques semaines et, si nécessaire, travailler avec l'IA pour itérer sur ce qu'ils trouvent. À terme, il pourrait même être possible pour Claude lui-même de réaliser les expériences en toute sécurité en contrôlant de manière autonome l'équipement de laboratoire, avec des mesures de sécurité appropriées, mais nous ne le faisons pas aujourd'hui (notre laboratoire est également une installation BSL1/BSL2 qui ne manipule pas de matériaux dangereux pour les humains). Plus largement, l'avancement biomédical comporte de nombreuses étapes — des découvertes fondamentales en biologie à la recherche translationnelle, la découverte de médicaments, les essais cliniques, et enfin la fourniture effective de médicaments et de soins de santé aux patients. Nous nous intéressons également à ces dernières étapes, mais le simple fait d'accélérer la première étape des découvertes biologiques fondamentales a le potentiel d'accélérer et d'élargir l'ensemble du processus. Améliorer notre compréhension de la biologie et affûter les outils des biologistes peut faire avancer toutes les étapes ultérieures, par exemple en identifiant de nouvelles cibles médicamenteuses, en trouvant de nouvelles modalités thérapeutiques, en permettant des mesures plus précises et en accélérant la boucle expérimentale qui, elle-même, accélère notre compréhension de la biologie. Cela n'accélérera pas en soi les délais des essais cliniques, mais si cela réussit, cela pourrait considérablement augmenter le nombre de candidats prometteurs qui entrent dans le processus — une augmentation du débit même si la latence demeure. Dans Machines of Loving Grace, j'ai écrit sur le potentiel de l'IA à « guérir la plupart des maladies en 5 à 10 ans » — un objectif qui semble impossible, mais que je crois à peine possible si l'IA est appliquée à chaque étape du processus. La première étape consiste à montrer que l'IA peut d'abord aider avec, et ensuite mener, des découvertes biologiques. La découverte de Claude est la dernière d'une série de travaux antérieurs connexes qui remontent à des décennies, commençant par des systèmes comme CRISPR, et se poursuivant avec des découvertes comme la recombinase en pont et VIPR ces dernières années. Récemment, l'intérêt s'est accru pour les systèmes basés sur les enzymes de la transcriptase inverse (RT), l'enzyme sous-jacente au système identifié par Claude. Et plus récemment, une équipe de Stanford travaillant indépendamment a décrit un nouveau système RT avec un ensemble non codant associé qui est à certains égards similaire à celui trouvé par Claude, bien qu'il s'agisse de systèmes distincts qui ont évolué indépendamment l'un de l'autre. Je crois que nous sommes au tout début de la découverte de tels systèmes et de leur développement en outils puissants pour la biotechnologie. Je suis fier des ressources qu'Anthropic a investies pour accélérer les bénéfices publics de l'IA par le biais des sciences de la vie, et nous visons à la fois à développer notre équipe de sciences de la vie et à travailler avec d'autres scientifiques pour étendre cette approche à un large éventail de problèmes. Si vous avez une proposition de collaboration de recherche ou si vous êtes intéressé à rejoindre notre équipe de sciences de la vie, n'hésitez pas à nous contacter. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude a découvert un système enzymatique jusqu'alors inconnu, caché dans l'ADN des bactériophages. À côté du gène de l'enzyme se trouve une longue séquence d'ADN répétitif — une structure qui ressemble quelque peu à CRISPR. Nous ne comprenons pas encore ce que fait ce système, mais seule une poignée de systèmes connus partagent ses caractéristiques, et tous sont capables de couper, copier et coller l'ADN. Historiquement, la découverte de tels systèmes programmables a contribué à révolutionner la médecine. CRISPR, par exemple, est maintenant la base des médicaments génétiques. Mais il faudra beaucoup plus de travail pour savoir ce que fait ce système et s'il peut être utilisé de manière similaire. Lisez-en plus : anthropic.com/news/claude-di…

In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. idees.text_fr: 2/2 Deuxièmement, sur la communication autour de l'IA. Je ne suis pas d'accord pour dire que ma communication a été disproportionnellement négative. En fait, elle a été à peu près également équilibrée entre les risques et les bénéfices : j'ai écrit un essai majeur sur chacun, et même dans les interviews où je discute des risques, je m'assure de mentionner fréquemment les incroyables bénéfices ainsi que de proposer des solutions possibles aux risques (les courts extraits de mes interviews qui finissent sur les réseaux sociaux ont tendance à être disproportionnellement négatifs, car cela génère des clics). En fait, j'ai écrit "Machines of Loving Grace" parce que je ne trouvais pas que l'industrie de l'IA brossait un tableau suffisamment inspirant de la manière dont la technologie pourrait transformer radicalement le monde pour le mieux. L'essentiel de l'essai est consacré à réfuter le scepticisme quant au potentiel de l'IA dans la santé et la biologie, et à montrer pourquoi je pense qu'il sera réellement possible de guérir la plupart des maladies humaines en 5 à 10 ans, aussi fou que cela puisse paraître aux gens ordinaires et même aux biologistes (j'en étais un !). Et, si vous lisez mon essai le plus récent ("Policy on the AI Exponential"), je discute de propositions concrètes pour rationaliser le processus de la FDA afin de s'assurer que le déluge de médicaments accélérés par l'IA ne soit pas ralenti par le processus réglementaire. Je ressens l'urgence ici : j'ai perdu mon père à cause de l'hépatite C quelques années seulement avant le développement d'antiviraux à action directe (sofosbuvir), qui guérissent 95% des patients et l'auraient probablement guéri. Je suis d'accord pour dire que le public a une vision négative de l'IA (et que c'est un gros problème), mais je ne pense pas que cela soit principalement causé par moi ou par tout autre leader de l'IA avertissant des risques de l'IA. Je pense que c'est fondamentalement une crise de confiance. Je pense que les gens ordinaires ne font pas confiance aux entreprises, aux gouvernements ou à l'industrie technologique et soupçonnent toujours que nous concoctons une nouvelle façon de les arnaquer. Les causes de cela remontent à des décennies et l'IA n'en est que la dernière itération. Je ne pense pas qu'une campagne marketing tape-à-l'œil avec une tournure positive (que certains ont préconisé à Anthropic de faire) soit le moyen de regagner cette confiance — à ce stade, dire que l'IA va guérir le cancer est plus un cliché qu'une source d'inspiration, et la plupart des gens pensent que c'est trompeur. Ce qui fonctionnera, c'est de *réellement guérir le cancer*. Je pense que la critique la plus juste des entreprises d'IA, y compris Anthropic, est que nous n'avons pas encore tenu nos grandes promesses de bénéficier au monde. Cela nous incombe entièrement, et je pense que c'est la critique que vous devriez faire, au lieu de tout ce qui concerne la communication et le marketing. Nous faisons cependant de notre mieux pour y remédier : Anthropic intensifie très rapidement ses efforts en biologie et en médecine, et nous espérons avoir des résultats incroyables dans les années à venir et quelques aperçus précoces dans les mois à venir. Lorsque nous aurons accompli quelque chose de réel, le monde entier en entendra parler, aussi fort que possible, je vous le promets. Mais jusque-là, je ne veux pas faire de promesses en l'air, et en attendant, je me sens obligé de parler honnêtement des risques très réels de l'IA et de la manière de les aborder. L'honnêteté est la bonne chose sur le fond, et en termes de crédibilité et de confiance publiques, ce n'est pas pire que, et pourrait en fait être mieux qu'une approche qui ignore ou détourne l'attention des risques qui les gens instinctivement comprennent sont réels.

In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

idees.text_fr: 1/2 Merci Gavin pour cet échange particulièrement réfléchi. Je ne passe généralement pas beaucoup de temps sur les réseaux sociaux, mais je voulais m'engager ici car cela met en lumière le cœur d'une conversation importante. Premièrement, sur la régulation, je pense que "soit la concentrer entre les mains de quelques entreprises et politiciens choisis via la régulation, soit la distribuer largement" est un faux dilemme. Je sais qu'il y a une sorte de raccourci dans la Silicon Valley où régulation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir, mais j'ai toujours trouvé cela être une image trop simplifiée du monde. Beaucoup de gens en dehors de cette bulle pensent que la régulation est quelque chose qui contraint le pouvoir des entreprises et profite aux gens ordinaires. Je ne suis pas nécessairement d'accord avec cette perspective non plus, je pense plutôt que c'est compliqué et que cela dépend vraiment de ce en quoi consiste la "régulation". Mais en particulier, je pense que ceux qui adoptent le cadre "régulation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir" sous-estiment souvent le pouvoir décentralisateur des processus institutionnels objectifs et équitables. Une analogie grossière est que le système judiciaire formel peut parfois sembler guindé et élitiste, mais il fait un bien meilleur travail de défense des droits des individus vulnérables que l'alternative, la justice de la foule. Au mieux, les institutions peuvent investir le pouvoir dans des idées plutôt que dans des personnes, et ainsi décentraliser ce pouvoir. C'est pourquoi Anthropic a toujours élaboré ses propositions politiques très soigneusement. Nous nous efforçons de faire des propositions qui désavantagent (ralentissent) les entreprises d'IA de pointe tout en *avantageant* les petits concurrents. La SB53 de Californie (que nous avons soutenue), et même la très critiquée SB 1047 (sur laquelle nous étions ambivalents), exemptent complètement toute entreprise en dessous d'un certain montant de revenus ou de coûts d'entraînement de modèle d'être couverte (c'était 500 millions de dollars pour la SB 53, moins pour la 1047 mais nous nous y sommes opposés). Plus récemment, le processus de test que nous avons préconisé auprès de la CAISI et de la Maison Blanche implique des tests plus rigoureux pour les modèles de pointe que pour les modèles non de pointe — quelque chose qui avantage différemment les challengers. De même, la lettre "Pacing the Frontier" envisage (ou du moins l'implémentation préférée d'Anthropic l'envisage) de moduler le rythme des meilleurs modèles sans contraindre ceux qui sont en train de rattraper leur retard. Cela nuit aux intérêts commerciaux des laboratoires de pointe et aide les challengers, y compris les modèles open-weights ! Dans l'ensemble, mon point de vue est que l'IA est *structurellement* une technologie qui tend à concentrer le pouvoir, pour des raisons qui n'ont rien à voir avec la régulation (plus à voir avec les implications extrêmes des lois d'échelle). Les modèles open-weights aident en partie à cela, mais sont loin d'être une solution suffisante car ils ne font que déplacer la concentration vers ceux qui ont le plus de calcul et de puces (qui sont grosso modo les laboratoires de pointe plus peut-être les fournisseurs de matériel). Par contre, je pense que les bonnes "règles du jeu" peuvent simultanément (a) adresser les risques cyber/bio/d'alignement de l'IA, (b) contraindre institutionnellement le pouvoir des entreprises d'IA de pointe, et (c) laisser de la place aux modèles open-weights tout en abordant les risques spécifiques qu'ils entraînent. D'ailleurs, je ne pense pas que les événements des derniers mois n'aient "pas abouti à [ma] voie réglementaire préférée". L'approche que l'administration Trump serait en train d'adopter — des tests avant déploiement pour les modèles de pointe, et aussi des tests des modèles open-weights lorsqu'ils se rapprochent de la frontière — est une approche que je soutiens fortement, bien sûr je dois en voir les détails pour en être sûr. Je soutiens également les idées de Demis Hassabis concernant une entité de type FINRA. Cela contraste avec il y a six mois, lorsque la plupart de l'industrie poussait encore à la préemption de toutes les réglementations étatiques et à aucune approche fédérale apparente.
idees.text_original: 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either.

outils.text_fr: Très bon événement parallèle. 0xturbanurban (@0xturbanurban) Hier soir, j'ai eu le plaisir d'assister à un événement intéressant organisé par @sfcompute et @jumptrading, axé sur l'espace du calcul (compute space). Quelques points clés à retenir : - Il y a une compréhension croissante qu'une plus grande liquidité sur les marchés du calcul nécessite la construction d'indices de référence unifiés, afin que les marchés sur mesure/de gré à gré (OTC) puissent être évalués comme une différence par rapport à un ensemble commun de repères, similaire à ce qui existe déjà dans le complexe énergétique (pensez aux qualités de brut et à l'électricité). Une partie de la discussion porte sur la question de savoir si cela émergera organiquement si des acteurs plus traditionnels (Citadel, Jump, banques de premier ordre) étendent leur offre OTC pour les couvertures bilatérales (en utilisant leurs propres prix), ou si cela nécessitera une partie indépendante (S&P, CME, etc.) pour valider et accorder de la crédibilité pour une adoption plus large. - La croissance massive de l'espace du calcul est largement soutenue par des opérations de financement structuré avec des mandats de couverture (similaires à ce que l'on voit dans le secteur pétrolier et gazier). Si quelqu'un avec un bilan important vous a prêté beaucoup d'argent, qui est susceptible de vous offrir des prix plus agressifs que son bras de vente et de trading ? - Le financement des assureurs-vie a été un élément clé de la construction des centres de données (on pourrait appeler cela l'appariement de la durée), avec un nombre croissant d'assureurs qui envisagent de couvrir le calcul. Une partie de cette exposition se trouve dans les portefeuilles de prêts hypothécaires, tandis que le plus grand segment est via les obligations d'entreprises ( $ORCL , $MSFT , $META , et $GOOG représentent près de 80% de la dette logicielle IG d'Athene). - Un certain nombre de personnes semblent pessimistes sur le long terme, principalement en raison de : * Craintes que des vendeurs en difficulté puissent inonder le marché si la croissance de l'IA ralentit (car il y a beaucoup de dettes garanties par des GPU à dénouer) * Les couvertures naturelles sont principalement des vendeurs, car les opérateurs ont besoin de revenus contractuels pour emprunter, ils vendent donc plus loin sur la courbe ; les acheteurs bloquent principalement les taux à court terme avec une demande marginale provenant d'une poignée de laboratoires dont les dépenses dépendent de leur capacité à toujours obtenir un financement * Les améliorations logicielles réduisent les besoins en heures GPU, tandis que les nouvelles puces déprécient la valeur de l'ancien matériel par unité de calcul : $NVDA sort une nouvelle génération environ chaque année (Blackwell Ultra, Rubin et Rubin Ultra). Cela dit, il semble que les anciennes puces restent utiles plus longtemps que la plupart des modèles de dépréciation ne le supposent, car l'inférence et les modèles plus petits permettent toujours une monétisation suffisante de l'ancien matériel. Il sera très intéressant de voir comment cet espace continue de mûrir, en particulier à mesure que de nouveaux marchés commencent à émerger pour le calcul réglé financièrement et physiquement. Un grand merci à @affaan et à l'équipe pour l'organisation !

Some brief takeaways: - There's an increasing understanding that greater liquidity in compute markets requires the construction of unifying benchmark indices, so that bespoke/OTC markets can be priced/quoted as a diff to a shared set of benchmarks, similar to what exists in the energy complex already (think crude grades and power). Part of the discussion is whether this will organically emerge if more traditional players (Citadel, Jump, blue-chip banks) expand their OTC offering for bilateral hedges (using their own prices), or require an independent party (S&P, CME, etc.) to validate and give credence for broader adoption. - Massive growth in the compute space is largely underpinned by structured financing trades with hedging mandates (similar to what you see in the oil and gas space). If someone with a sizable balance sheet just lent you a lot of money, who's likely to give you more aggressive pricing than their sales and trading arm? - Funding from life insurers has been a key part of the data center buildout (you could call it duration matching), with an increasing number of insurers considering hedging compute. Some of this exposure sits in mortgage books, while the biggest bucket is via corporate bonds ( $ORCL , $MSFT , $META , and $GOOG comprise nearly 80% of Athene's IG software debt). - Quite a few folks seem offered over on the backend of the curve, largely driven by: * Concerns that distressed sellers could flood the market if the AI growth story slows down (as there's a lot of GPU-backed debt to unwind) * Natural hedgers are mostly sellers, as operators need contracted revenue to borrow, so they sell further out on the curve; buyers mostly lock in near-term rates w/ marginal demand coming from a handful of labs whose spending is contingent on their ability to still tap into financing * Software improvements are reducing GPU-hour needs, all the while new chips are depreciating the value of old hardware per unit of compute: $NVDA is releasing a new gen roughly every year (Blackwell Ultra, Rubin, and Rubin Ultra). That said, it does look like old chips are staying useful longer than most depreciation models assume, since inference and smaller models still allow sufficient monetization of older hardware. It'll be quite exciting to see how the space continues to mature, especially as new marketplaces begin to emerge for financially and physically settled compute. Huge thanks to @affaan and team for organizing!
